verdict.winner: Asphalt shingles win on cost; natural slate wins on multi-generational lifespan
verdict.reasoning: Asphalt shingles beat natural slate when the ownership horizon is under 15 years or the budget caps near the $10,000 to $11,000 national asphalt-replacement benchmark, since asphalt installs at $5.50 to $11.00 per square foot.
verdict.alternate: Natural slate beats asphalt shingles when the home already carries slate or sits in a designated local historic district, where Standard 6 of the Secretary of the Interior's Standards directs an in-kind match rather than an asphalt substitute.

keyFacts: Natural slate lasts 60 to 150 years versus 20 to 30 years for asphalt shingles, per the InterNACHI Standard Estimated Life Expectancy Chart.
The National Slate Association rates ASTM S-1 grade slate at a 75-year minimum service life.
Asphalt life splits by type: 3-tab lasts about 20 years and architectural about 30 years, per the InterNACHI chart.
The NRCA notes actual asphalt shingle life varies up to 40% with climate, installation, and maintenance.

Asphalt is a light covering that loads any properly sheathed roof with no structural upgrade, while natural slate is a heavy quarried-stone covering whose structural load is reviewed before installation.
Natural slate requires non-ferrous solid copper or stainless-steel fasteners, because plain or galvanized steel rusts out long before the slate, per NPS Preservation Brief 29.
Natural slate outlasts its own fasteners and flashing, so failures trace to corroded fasteners or degraded valley flashing rather than the stone itself, per NPS Preservation Brief 29.
Asphalt shingles fail through wind-driven granule loss, edge and tab curling, and thermal-shock cracking along the cutouts, per NRCA and InterNACHI guidance.
On lower-grade stone, slate weathers to surface sugaring rather than structural cracking, per NRCA and the National Slate Association.
Natural slate reaches full replacement when 20% or more of its slates are broken, missing, or sliding, per NPS Preservation Brief 29.

Asphalt shingles reach full replacement when damage exceeds 25 to 30% of the roof area, per contractor consensus, with the 50% rule favoring replacement once one repair approaches half the replacement cost.
A single broken slate replaces for $50 to $300, per HomeGuide; slate repair averages near $1,400 within a $500 to $2,100 band.
Asphalt shingle repair runs $360 to $1,550 for minor patch or flashing work, per Angi.
A New Jersey roof leak repair runs $400 to $1,000, per HomeAdvisor, with NJ pricing about 10 to 15% above the national average.

Architectural asphalt shingles replicate slate's layered, dimensional profile, last about 30 years per the InterNACHI chart, and install at $6.50 to $11.00 per square foot in NJ per Josten Roofing, against natural slate's $10 to $30.
Slate is never walked on or coated to seal moisture; the stone is sounded, flipped, and reset rather than patched, per NPS Preservation Brief 29.

Natural slate is the in-kind material on a contributing structure in a designated local historic district, where Standard 6 of the Secretary of the Interior's Standards directs that a deteriorated slate roof be repaired or matched in kind rather than swapped for asphalt.
sources: InterNACHI Standard Estimated Life Expectancy Chart
NPS Preservation Brief 29 (Repair, Replacement, and Maintenance of Historic Slate Roofs)
N.J.S.A. 40:55D-107 (Certificate of Appropriateness / Historic Preservation Commission)
NJEDA / NJ Historic Property Reinvestment Program
njContext: Asphalt shingles install across northern New Jersey at $5.50 to $9.50 per square foot for 3-tab and $6.50 to $11.00 for architectural, per Josten Roofing's NJ figures.

Natural slate installs at $10 to $30 per square foot, roughly $1,500 per square, per NJ roofing guides, and is the highest-priced covering on the historic homes of Montclair, Glen Ridge, and Newark's landmark districts.

Asphalt shingles depend on an ice-and-water shield at the eaves, required at eaves with an ice-dam history and extending at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line, per IRC R905.1.2 as enforced under the NJ Uniform Construction Code (N.J.A.C. 5:23).

In NJ freeze-thaw climate, natural slate failures trace to corroded fasteners and degraded valley flashing rather than the stone, while asphalt shingles crack and curl after years of freeze-thaw, per NRCA and InterNACHI guidance.

Natural slate on a landmark commercial property in Newark's James Street Commons or Lincoln Park district triggers a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic Preservation Commission, per N.J.S.A. 40:55D-107, before a roofing-material change.

A partial asphalt swap on a contributing structure in a designated local historic district can require a Certificate of Appropriateness; below 20% slate failure, NPS Preservation Brief 29 favors selective slate repair over wholesale change.

The federal 20% Historic Rehabilitation Tax Credit and the NJ Historic Property Reinvestment Program apply only to income-producing properties; owner-occupied homes do not qualify, per the NPS and the NJ DEP Historic Preservation Office.
Flat commercial roofs use single-ply membrane systems rather than either steep-slope material, matching the low-slope geometry.
positioning: Position Newark Quality Roofing as a registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor (N.J.S.A. 56:8-136), insured, offering a free written estimate, that installs both asphalt and natural slate across Essex County. NQR reviews the home's structural load before specifying slate (a heavy quarried-stone covering) and matches in-kind material on contributing structures in designated local historic districts per Standard 6, coordinating any required Certificate of Appropriateness. Frame warranty honestly as two parts: a manufacturer material warranty plus NQR's own written workmanship warranty, never as manufacturer certification tiers. Never claim a roofing license (NJ issues none for roofing) and never claim manufacturer-certification status not held by the business.

buyersGuide.h1: Which Is Better: Asphalt vs Slate Roofing?
buyersGuide.directAnswerThesis: Asphalt shingles win on upfront cost ($5.50-$11.00/sq ft, 20-30 year life); natural slate wins on lifespan (60-150 years per InterNACHI). The deciding factor is ownership horizon and whether the home is in a historic district.

expertPicks.h1: What Do NJ Roofers Recommend for Asphalt vs Slate Roofing?
expertPicks.directAnswerThesis: The standards favor in-kind slate on historic homes (Standard 6) and slate for multi-generational life (60-150 years, InterNACHI); for budget or short-horizon homes the standards-backed recommendation is quality architectural asphalt with proper detailing.
